doc.title: Eddie Marshall interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 8, 2002

chapter: Family and early playing in Springfield
title: Uncle Roddy's records turn him to bebop
summary: Uncle Roddy left jazz records when drafted; hearing Miles Davis made him leave the R&B band.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Yeah, yeah, yeah. It was, I don’t know, anyhow so I started playing with Cookie and the Seven Sharps and Cookie is still alive, he’s like eighty something years old. And that was it. And I Just stayed with that until I was 18. And then I had an uncle, my Uncle Roddy, who got drafted into the Army. Actually he got drafted into the Marines during the Korean War which was really — I think he was drafted and they gave him a choice or something. But he ended up a draftee in the Marines. And he was a jazz fanatic. So he left, you know I was the only one he could leave his records with, and they were all jazz records. There was “Charlie Parker with Strings,” I think it was Max Roach — no it was “Milestones,” the old “Milestones,” with Miles and Sonny Rollins, and there was another one — “The Modern Jazz Quartet” or something. Anyway well I heard Miles Davis and that did it. I was totally gone for jazz. I couldn’t play with Cookie anymore. Because, you know I remember the last few jobs I played with Cookie I was so obsessed with bebop I’m trying to play bebop in the rhythm & blues tunes. And they are looking at me, you know there’s a groove. First of all I didn’t fit, and I didn’t even know how to do it right anyway.
That’s so interesting that you got pulled out of your father’s mode into this thing, and then out of that thing.
